paragraphs: Many learning problems have two objectives: fit the observed data and satisfy an additional preference expressed through an auxiliary loss. A common solution adds the losses together after multiplying one by a manually chosen weight. This paper questions that approach, highlighting both the tuning burden and its theoretical shortcomings when the objectives are non-convex.

The authors instead study constrained optimization, which expresses the relationship between objectives through a constraint. They give particular attention to lexicographic optimization: first prioritize the main loss, then improve the secondary loss within the set of solutions that already optimize the main one. In this formulation, the secondary objective cannot justify moving outside that optimal set.

The proposed dynamic barrier gradient descent algorithm addresses both constrained and lexicographic optimization within one framework. The authors establish convergence for general non-convex functions. The contribution is therefore a method and theoretical foundation for handling ordered objectives, with the trade-off encoded in the optimization problem rather than solely in a manually weighted sum.
neurips-2021-automatic-and-harmless-regu.tldr: A dynamic barrier gradient method handles constrained and priority-ordered objectives, with convergence results for non-convex functions.

paragraphs: Few-shot meta-learning aims to use experience across tasks to learn effectively on a new task with very few examples. Existing PAC-Bayesian analyses struggled to explain the improvements seen in this setting. The paper identifies a specific mismatch: those theories assume that example counts in previously observed tasks and target tasks follow the same distribution.

The authors relax that assumption and derive two PAC-Bayesian bounds designed for few-shot learning. This makes the theoretical setup better reflect situations where experience comes from tasks with different amounts of data than the eventual target tasks. They also show that the existing MAML and Reptile algorithms can be derived from these bounds, connecting established methods to the revised analysis.

The same framework leads to PACMAML, a new algorithm described as computationally efficient. The authors report that it outperforms existing meta-learning algorithms on several few-shot benchmarks. Together, the results provide a theoretical account of familiar algorithms under more appropriate data-count assumptions and a new method whose reported benchmark performance supports the usefulness of that account.
neurips-2021-bridging-the-gap-between-pr.tldr: Relaxing a task-size assumption yields few-shot PAC-Bayesian bounds that explain MAML and Reptile and motivate the PACMAML algorithm.

paragraphs: Models trained for adversarial robustness can also improve performance on some downstream tasks, but the mechanism behind these benefits remains unclear. This paper investigates robustness by examining the linear components of neural networks. The aim is to identify statistical structure associated with robust models that may be obscured by the full network's nonlinear operations.

The authors remove or replace nonlinear components, including batch normalization, maximum pooling, and activation layers, to examine linearized subnetworks. They observe a pronounced hierarchical clustering effect in comprehensively robust models. This suggests that studying the remaining linear structure provides a useful perspective on robustness, alongside evaluating how the intact model responds to adversarial attacks.

Building on these observations, the authors develop a clustering strategy and apply it to domain adaptation and robustness improvement. Their experiments support the strategy's effectiveness and the interpretation motivating it. The stated contribution combines an observed structural property with practical applications; the abstract presents clustering as a way to understand and exploit robustness, without establishing it as a complete causal explanation.
neurips-2021-clustering-effect-of-advers.tldr: Robust models exhibit hierarchical clustering in their linearized subnetworks, motivating a strategy for domain adaptation and robustness improvement.

paragraphs: Active learning seeks to learn from a stream of examples while requesting relatively few labels. This paper studies binary classification when an adversary can corrupt labels and the learner does not know which labels are affected. The timing matters: the adversary decides whether to corrupt a label before the learner observes the corresponding sample.

For a benign corruption setting that also includes model misspecification, the authors show that a small change to RobustCAL's hypothesis elimination threshold preserves nearly the label efficiency available without corruption. However, that modified algorithm can fail under more general corruption. They therefore introduce another algorithm with correctness guarantees that do not require assuming corruptions are absent or benign.

The new method retains minimax label complexity when labels are uncorrupted. With corruption, it requires roughly an additional number of labels proportional to the total corruption count, up to logarithmic factors. Its error guarantee scales as the target accuracy plus the fraction of corrupted samples. This quantifies how both labeling cost and achievable accuracy deteriorate as corruption increases.
neurips-2021-corruption-robust-active-le.tldr: A streaming active-learning algorithm preserves optimal label efficiency without corruption and bounds the additional cost and error caused by adversarial labels.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a brain's cortical surface requires producing a detailed geometric object from a three-dimensional image. CorticalFlow approaches this by deforming a reference mesh toward the target surface. Starting from a template makes preserving its topological structure an explicit part of the learning problem, alongside matching the object visible in the image.

The model learns diffeomorphic transformations, which provide a topology-preserving framework for the deformation. Its implementation uses a flow ordinary differential equation and has a small GPU memory footprint, supporting surfaces with several hundred thousand vertices. Because representing a continuous transformation on a discrete mesh can still introduce topological errors, the authors also derive numerical conditions that improve the resulting mesh's manifoldness.

On cortical surface reconstruction, the authors report superior surfaces compared with the current state of the art and a computation-time reduction from nine and a half minutes to one second. They also emphasize anatomically plausible outputs. These findings connect computational efficiency with geometric validity, addressing both the expense of detailed reconstruction and a stated obstacle to its clinical relevance.
neurips-2021-corticalflow-a-diffeomorphi.tldr: CorticalFlow deforms a reference mesh through topology-preserving flows to reconstruct detailed, anatomically plausible cortical surfaces quickly.

paragraphs: A mixture-of-experts model routes each input to a selection of specialized networks. In multi-task learning, this provides a way to share model capacity across tasks while allowing different inputs to use different experts. The routing rule matters: popular sparse gates such as Top-k are not smooth, which can create difficulties for gradient-based optimization and prediction quality.

DSelect-k replaces that routing rule with a sparse gate that is continuously differentiable. Its binary encoding formulation allows training with first-order methods such as stochastic gradient descent while explicitly controlling how many experts are selected. The approach therefore addresses the interaction between discrete expert selection and the smooth updates used to train the surrounding network.

The authors evaluate the gate on synthetic and real multi-task datasets containing up to 128 tasks. They report statistically significant improvements in prediction and expert selection over popular gates. In a large recommender system, predictive performance improves by more than 22% relative to Top-k. These are empirical findings from the studied settings, supporting differentiable routing as a useful design choice.
neurips-2021-dselect-k-differentiable-se.tldr: DSelect-k makes sparse expert selection continuously differentiable while controlling the number of selected experts, with reported gains in multi-task learning.

paragraphs: Language instructions can describe tasks that require many actions before an agent receives a reward. Such sparse feedback makes reinforcement learning expensive because the agent may need many episodes to discover useful behavior. ELLA addresses this problem by using relationships between high-level instructions and simpler instructions to shape rewards during exploration.

The method has two classifiers with different responsibilities. A termination classifier recognizes when the agent has completed a low-level instruction; it is trained offline using instruction and terminal-state pairs. A relevance classifier learns which low-level instructions are associated with success on the larger task. This second classifier learns online, so ELLA does not require an explicit decomposition of each high-level instruction into smaller instructions.

The authors test ELLA in BabyAI environments with different instruction complexities and degrees of reward sparsity. They report improved sample efficiency relative to language-based reward shaping and traditional reinforcement learning methods. The results support learning which simpler accomplishments are useful during training, making language abstractions a source of guidance when the task's own rewards arrive infrequently.
neurips-2021-ella-exploration-through-le.tldr: ELLA improves exploration by learning which completed low-level language instructions are relevant to sparse-reward, high-level tasks.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation adjusts a model when its new inputs differ from the data used to train it. This paper considers the source-free setting: the pretrained model is available, but its original training data are not. The authors observe that target examples can still form clear feature clusters even when the source-trained classifier no longer aligns well with them.

Their method uses those clusters through local affinity, a measure of how strongly nearby target examples should influence one another. It encourages highly related examples to receive consistent labels and gives greater weight to reciprocal neighbors. A self-regularization loss reduces the harmful influence of noisy neighbors, while expanded neighborhoods contribute broader context with smaller affinity weights.

Experiments support the value of target feature structure as information for adaptation. The authors report that combining local, reciprocal, and expanded neighborhoods captures this structure efficiently, achieving state-of-the-art performance on several image and point-cloud recognition datasets. The approach matters because it extracts adaptation guidance from relationships within the available target data when revisiting the source dataset is impossible.
neurips-2021-exploiting-the-intrinsic-ne.tldr: Target-data neighborhoods guide adaptation of a pretrained classifier without access to its source data.

paragraphs: Expectation Maximization is a standard method for fitting models that contain unobserved variables. Applying it across distributed datasets introduces practical problems: communication can be expensive, devices may participate only intermittently, and their data distributions may differ. This paper introduces FedEM as an extension of EM to the federated learning setting that addresses these issues.

FedEM reduces communication by compressing appropriately defined complete-data sufficient statistics. These statistics are the quantities the method uses to summarize information relevant to estimation. The algorithm accommodates partial device participation and heterogeneous datasets. The authors also develop a version with variance reduction, adding a mechanism for reducing variability in the estimation procedure.

For both versions, the paper derives finite-time complexity bounds for smooth, non-convex problems. These results characterize computational progress without restricting the objective to a convex setting. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings, and an application fills in missing values in federated biodiversity-monitoring data. The contribution brings communication-aware distributed computation to latent-variable inference while explicitly accounting for uneven data and device availability.
neurips-2021-federated-em-with-heterogen.tldr: FedEM adapts Expectation Maximization to federated data through compressed statistics, partial participation support, and an optional variance-reduction scheme.

paragraphs: Standard transformer attention has time and memory costs that grow quadratically with sequence length. FMMformer draws inspiration from the fast multipole method, which accelerates particle simulations by treating nearby interactions directly and distant interactions more coarsely. The paper transfers that division of labor to attention, giving nearby and faraway positions different mathematical representations.

Near-field attention uses a banded matrix, concentrating its detailed structure around nearby sequence positions. Far-field attention uses a low-rank matrix to represent longer-range interactions compactly. Together, these components give attention computation linear time and memory complexity in sequence length. The design keeps both local and distant interactions while changing how much structure is used to represent each.

The authors analyze and evaluate FMMformers on Long Range Arena and language-modeling benchmarks. They report that the models can surpass standard transformer accuracy as well as reduce computational complexity. Across five Long Range Arena tasks, average classification accuracy is 60.74%, compared with 58.70% for the standard transformer. This example shows that the reported efficiency improvement need not come with lower accuracy in the tested setting.
neurips-2021-fmmformer-efficient-and-fle.tldr: FMMformer combines banded local attention with low-rank distant attention for linear scaling and reported accuracy gains.

paragraphs: Simple pruning methods can substantially shrink large neural networks, but explaining why trained networks tolerate this compression is harder. This paper links compressibility to two possible properties of stochastic gradient descent: weights becoming independent in an infinite-width mean-field limit, and training iterates approaching a heavy-tailed stationary distribution when the step-size-to-batch-size ratio is large.

The main guarantee assumes that both properties occur together. Under that assumption, the authors prove a form of compressibility measured using an l-p criterion. They also show that errors from magnitude pruning, singular-value pruning, and node pruning can become arbitrarily small as network size increases. Thus, the result depends on a particular combination of training behavior and growing model size.

The paper additionally derives generalization bounds consistent with lower generalization error for more compressible networks. Its theory and numerical studies indicate that large step-size-to-batch-size ratios introduce heavy tails, which combine with overparameterization to produce compressibility. The contribution is a conditional explanation connecting optimization dynamics, removable model structure, and generalization, rather than treating successful pruning as an isolated empirical observation.
neurips-2021-heavy-tails-in-sgd-and-comp.tldr: Under joint independence and heavy-tail assumptions for SGD, increasingly large networks admit pruning with vanishing compression error.

paragraphs: When multiple agents perceive a scene together, exchanging information can improve detection but consumes communication bandwidth. This paper learns a collaboration graph that adapts information sharing to agents' poses and the spatial regions that matter. Its aim is a better balance between perception performance and the amount of information agents must communicate.

Training uses a teacher with holistic-view inputs and early collaboration to guide a student that collaborates through intermediate features from single-view inputs. The student's features after collaboration are encouraged to match the teacher's corresponding features. Graph edges have matrix-valued weights, allowing attention between agents to vary across spatial regions instead of assigning one uniform importance to an entire connection.

At inference, only the student network, DiscoNet, is needed. The authors evaluate multi-agent 3D object detection on V2X-Sim 1.0, a dataset synthesized through CARLA and SUMO co-simulation. They report a better performance-bandwidth trade-off than state-of-the-art collaborative methods. The findings suggest that agents sharing the student model can approach a holistic-view teacher's performance through selective, learned collaboration.
neurips-2021-learning-distilled-collabor.tldr: DiscoNet learns spatially selective collaboration from a holistic-view teacher to improve multi-agent perception's performance-bandwidth trade-off.

paragraphs: Cross-modal matching learns relationships between different kinds of data, such as images and text. Many methods assume that training pairs correctly correspond, but obtaining fully aligned data can be extremely costly or impossible. This paper focuses on noisy correspondence: the error lies in pairing two samples together, rather than assigning an incorrect category label to one sample.

The proposed Noisy Correspondence Rectifier first divides training data into clean and noisy partitions using the memorization behavior of neural networks. It then uses an adaptive prediction model to rectify correspondence through co-teaching. This separates identifying questionable pairings from correcting their influence, making correspondence reliability an explicit part of learning.

The authors use image-text matching to demonstrate the method and report experiments on Flickr30K, MS-COCO, and Conceptual Captions that support its effectiveness. The contribution broadens the treatment of training noise to include relationships between modalities. Its stated findings show the usefulness of addressing mismatched pairs directly in the evaluated matching tasks, where assuming every provided association is correct would overlook the central source of noise.
neurips-2021-learning-with-noisy-corresp.tldr: NCR identifies and rectifies mismatched multimodal training pairs, with effectiveness demonstrated on image-text matching datasets.

paragraphs: A multi-armed bandit learner must balance trying uncertain actions against choosing actions that already appear rewarding. This paper studies that exploration problem across many related tasks. Each task comes with descriptive features, called metadata, which provide a basis for sharing knowledge rather than learning every task in isolation.

The authors use Bayesian hierarchical models to represent relationships among tasks. On top of that framework, they design a Thompson sampling algorithm that learns those relationships while using shared information to choose actions. The objective is to reduce cumulative regret, the accumulated shortfall from choices that earn less reward than the relevant best choices.

The paper analyzes concrete versions for Gaussian and Bernoulli bandits. Its Bayes regret result for Gaussian bandits explicitly demonstrates benefits from sharing information, and experiments further support the method. The central contribution is a framework in which task descriptions inform exploration across tasks. This gives metadata an active role in deciding what to try next, while the learner continues updating its understanding of how tasks are related.
neurips-2021-metadata-based-multi-task-b.tldr: A Bayesian hierarchical Thompson sampling method uses task metadata to share information and improve exploration across related bandit problems.

paragraphs: Language changes as the world changes: people discuss new events, facts, and subjects, and their ways of expressing them evolve. Standard language-model evaluations often use training and evaluation text from overlapping periods. This paper examines a more temporally separated setting, asking how well models predict text produced after their training period has ended.

The authors find that Transformer-XL models perform worse on this future text and that the deterioration grows with elapsed time. Increasing model size alone does not resolve the problem in their study. Continually incorporating new information can mitigate the decline, indicating that keeping knowledge current matters alongside expanding the capacity of a fixed model.

The paper releases streaming language-modeling benchmarks based on WMT and arXiv to make temporal evaluation easier to study. Its findings motivate training and evaluation procedures that account for changing language and knowledge. For applications requiring current factual information, the results show why strong performance on temporally overlapping data may give an incomplete picture of how a model will perform after deployment.
neurips-2021-mind-the-gap-assessing-temp.tldr: Transformer-XL performance degrades on increasingly future text, while continual updates can mitigate a problem that model size alone does not solve.

paragraphs: Convolutional neural networks can achieve strong task performance while remaining vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Adversarial training can improve robustness, but it introduces a trade-off with standard accuracy. This paper approaches that trade-off through architecture, starting with a backbone network whose ordinary predictive accuracy is already satisfactory.

The proposed neural architecture dilation algorithm introduces an architectural addition intended to improve robustness with minimal computational overhead. Preserving the backbone's standard performance is a design goal, alongside making it more resistant to adversarial inputs. The authors motivate the algorithm through theoretical analyses of both standard and adversarial error bounds, linking the architectural proposal to the two performance criteria it must balance.

Experiments on real-world datasets and benchmark networks support the algorithm's effectiveness in balancing accuracy and robustness. The findings indicate that architectural changes can contribute to this balance in the studied settings. The abstract frames compatibility with standard accuracy as an aim of the method; it does not claim that every backbone receives robustness improvements with no accuracy cost.
neurips-2021-neural-architecture-dilatio.tldr: Neural architecture dilation seeks to improve adversarial robustness with little computational overhead while maintaining a useful balance with standard accuracy.

paragraphs: Link prediction asks whether two nodes in a graph should be connected. This paper represents a node pair through the paths connecting it: edge representations combine into a representation for each path, and those path representations combine into an overall pair representation. The formulation generalizes familiar path-based reasoning through flexible notions of multiplication and summation.

A generalized Bellman-Ford algorithm makes this path formulation computationally tractable. NBFNet then learns three parts of that algorithm: an Indicator function specifying the boundary condition, a Message function combining information along paths, and an Aggregate function combining contributions. This turns the structure of a classical graph algorithm into a trainable representation-learning framework.

The framework includes many traditional path-based methods and applies to graphs with either one or multiple relation types, including knowledge graphs. It supports both transductive and inductive settings. Experiments in these settings report large improvements over existing methods and state-of-the-art results. The contribution shows how learning the operators within a path-based algorithm can provide a flexible approach to predicting links across different graph types.
neurips-2021-neural-bellman-ford-network.tldr: NBFNet learns the operators of a generalized Bellman-Ford algorithm to represent node pairs through paths and predict graph links.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from a fixed dataset even when its policy would visit different situations. Conservative methods try to keep learning in trustworthy regions. However, restricting policy search can limit generalization, while forward model-generated trajectories can drift into poorly supported regions when estimates of conservatism are unreliable.

ROMI changes the direction of model-based imagination. It learns reverse dynamics together with a reverse policy, generating rollouts that lead toward target goal states already present in the offline dataset. These imagined trajectories augment the data used by a model-free learner. The approach aims to extend learning beyond recorded experience while grounding generated behavior in destinations supported by the dataset.

The framework can be combined with existing model-free algorithms. The authors report more conservative behavior and state-of-the-art performance on offline reinforcement-learning benchmarks. These empirical findings support reverse imagination as a way to balance generalization with caution. The key contribution is using the direction of generated trajectories to inform that balance, rather than relying only on conservative estimates attached to forward predictions.
neurips-2021-offline-reinforcement-learn.tldr: ROMI augments offline reinforcement-learning data with reverse-generated trajectories leading to dataset-supported goals, enabling more conservative generalization.

paragraphs: This paper studies functions that apply a one-dimensional periodic function to an affine projection of Gaussian input data. Despite their simple form, learning them with noisy labels can be computationally difficult. The authors connect this difficulty to worst-case lattice problems underlying lattice-based cryptography, extending earlier hardness results beyond gradient-based and Statistical Query algorithms.

Their reduction shows that a polynomial-time learner under polynomially small label noise would imply a polynomial-time quantum algorithm for those lattice problems. The learning-hardness conclusion therefore depends on the associated cryptographic assumptions. Its scope is broad with respect to learning algorithms: avoiding gradients or Statistical Queries does not by itself escape the stated noisy-learning barrier.

Noise is crucial to this conclusion. Using LLL lattice basis reduction, the authors give a polynomial-time learner for certain function families under exponentially small adversarial noise. Without noise, the algorithm also solves CLWE detection and phase retrieval with an optimal d+1 samples. The results distinguish noise regimes and show why computational hardness cannot be inferred from the function's form alone.
neurips-2021-on-the-cryptographic-hardne.tldr: Learning noisy periodic neurons is hard under lattice-based cryptographic assumptions, while certain families become efficiently learnable with much smaller noise.

paragraphs: Double descent describes a pattern in which test error falls again after model size becomes sufficiently large. This paper investigates how optimization contributes to that pattern in least-squares regression. Instead of analyzing only a final algebraic solution, it studies gradient descent and how its learning dynamics change with model size.

The authors derive an excess-risk bound involving the smallest nonzero eigenvalue of the input features' sample covariance matrix. The bound's dependence on this quantity has a double-descent form. Their analysis separates optimization effects from generalization effects, making it possible to ask which part of learning accounts for the shape of the error curve.

In the noiseless regression setting they study, double descent is explained entirely by optimization-related quantities. The authors present this as a possible explanation within least squares, rather than a universal account of neural-network behavior. They also empirically investigate neural networks by examining covariance spectra of intermediate-layer features. That exploration asks whether the spectral behavior predicted in the simpler setting appears in learned neural representations.
neurips-2021-on-the-role-of-optimization.tldr: A least-squares analysis separates optimization from generalization and attributes noiseless double descent to optimization-related spectral quantities.

paragraphs: Training a neural network typically relies on a hand-designed optimization procedure to find its parameters. This paper asks whether experience from other networks can instead support directly predicting useful parameters for a new architecture. The authors introduce DeepNets-1M, a large dataset of diverse architectural computation graphs, and study this problem on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.

Their hypernetwork uses graph neural-network advances to process architectures and predict parameters in a single forward pass. The reported prediction takes a fraction of a second even on a CPU. This makes the architecture itself an input to a learned parameter-producing model, allowing the method to address previously unseen networks with varied structures.

For example, the method predicts all 24 million parameters of a ResNet-50 that achieves 60% accuracy on CIFAR-10. Some evaluated networks approach 50% top-5 accuracy on ImageNet. The model also learns representations useful for analyzing architectures. These findings suggest a possible route toward more computationally efficient network training, while the paper presents that broader shift as a potential outcome.
neurips-2021-parameter-prediction-for-un.tldr: A graph-based hypernetwork predicts useful parameters for unseen neural architectures in a single fast forward pass.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a rank-one signal from rotationally invariant noise, a broader setting than Gaussian noise. Principal Component Analysis provides a natural starting estimate, while Approximate Message Passing has the potential to improve its accuracy. Previous AMP analysis, however, required an initialization correlated with the signal but independent of the noise, which can be unrealistic.

The authors initialize AMP with PCA and rigorously characterize its asymptotic performance. This explicitly handles a starting estimate constructed from the noisy observations. In their broader noise setting, every AMP iteration needs a specific term accounting for the PCA initialization. That differs from the Gaussian case, where the initialization affects only the first iteration.

The proof uses an artificial two-phase AMP process that first approximates PCA and then reproduces the actual AMP procedure. Numerical simulations agree closely with the theoretical predictions, supporting the analysis of this practical initialization. The results also point toward further work on Bayes-optimal performance; the abstract identifies that as an open direction rather than an achieved guarantee.
neurips-2021-pca-initialization-for-appr.tldr: PCA-initialized AMP receives a rigorous asymptotic analysis for rotationally invariant noise, with initialization corrections needed at every iteration.

paragraphs: Logistic regression can support unreliable statistical inference when the number of features is a substantial fraction of the number of observations. In this regime, conventional large-sample approximations for the maximum likelihood estimator behave poorly. Existing high-dimensional corrections address this problem, but implementing them requires estimating a signal strength that depends on unknown model parameters.

SLOE makes the correction more practical by expressing it in terms of corrupted signal strength, a quantity depending only on estimated parameters. The authors propose an estimator for this quantity and prove its consistency in the relevant high-dimensional regime. This reparameterization replaces the difficult unknown-parameter input with a quantity that can be estimated from the fitted model.

The paper reports accurate dimensionality correction in finite samples and computation that is orders of magnitude faster than the ProbeFrontier heuristic. Applications use the UCI Heart Disease dataset and UK Biobank genomics data to illustrate why routine correction matters. The contribution is a faster route to established high-dimensional inference corrections, supported by an asymptotic guarantee and empirical finite-sample results.
neurips-2021-sloe-a-faster-method-for-st.tldr: SLOE efficiently estimates the quantity needed to correct high-dimensional logistic-regression inference, with consistency and finite-sample accuracy results.

paragraphs: Recovering a low-rank matrix becomes difficult when observations contain both noise and outliers. Existing formulations such as stable Principal Component Pursuit can achieve useful reconstruction guarantees, but their parameter choices depend on the noise level. This paper addresses the practical problem that the noise level may be unknown before reconstruction begins.

Square Root Principal Component Pursuit takes inspiration from the square root Lasso. The authors show that one universal regularization-parameter choice is sufficient to obtain reconstruction error proportional to the unknown noise level. This removes the need to know that level when selecting the parameter, while still making the reconstruction guarantee responsive to how noisy the observations are.

Experiments on simulated and real data support the method's effectiveness. In simulations, the same parameter choice gives near-optimal performance across a range of noise levels. The observed performance is better than the paper's somewhat loose theoretical bound suggests. The contribution therefore combines a noise-independent parameter rule with a recovery guarantee and empirical evidence that the rule remains effective across varying noise conditions.
neurips-2021-square-root-principal-compo.tldr: Square Root PCP recovers low-rank matrices with one noise-independent regularization choice and error proportional to the unknown noise level.

paragraphs: Neural population recordings contain changing activity associated with behavior as well as other sources of variation. Latent dynamics models try to explain those recordings through a smaller set of hidden processes. This paper develops Targeted Neural Dynamical Modeling to jointly describe neural activity and simultaneously measured behavior while allowing nonlinear dynamics.

TNDM separates its latent dynamics into behaviorally relevant and behaviorally irrelevant components. A flexible linear decoder uses the relevant components to reconstruct behavior. A separate linear decoder uses both components to reconstruct neural activity without a time lag. This structure gives the model a way to preserve variation needed to explain neural recordings while distinguishing the part useful for explaining behavior.

The authors implement the model as a sequential variational autoencoder. They validate it on simulated recordings and premotor and motor cortex recordings from a monkey performing a center-out reaching task. TNDM learns low-dimensional dynamics that strongly predict behavior without sacrificing its fit to neural data. The result supports joint modeling as a way to make neural representations behaviorally informative while retaining explanatory coverage of the recordings.
neurips-2021-targeted-neural-dynamical-m.tldr: TNDM separates behaviorally relevant and irrelevant nonlinear neural dynamics, predicting behavior while preserving fit to neural recordings.
